paras: The attempted lynching of Perry Drake took place in September 1888 at Spencer, Roane County, West Virginia, where a mob tried to take Drake, on trial for the murder of the Rev. Thomas Ryan, from officers and threatened to lynch him. Threats against him continued in court and on the streets until the jury failed to agree, and no one was killed. Wire dispatches carried the story to papers as far away as New York and Ohio under headlines promising a lynching.

According to a Parkersburg dispatch, a band of robbers had come to Ryan's home in Roane County the previous fall and demanded his money, and Ryan was shot dead in the fight that followed. Citizens then lynched two men described as Drake's alleged accomplices, whose names the reports give differently as George and Bob Duffy or as Chess Coon and Bot Duff. Drake was captured about the same time but was saved from the lynchers and sent to the Charleston jail.

The trial opened at Spencer in early September, though the reports disagree on the day. A Parkersburg wire dated September 6 said that on the way from the jail to the court-room that morning the mob tried to drag the prisoner from the officers and threatened to lynch him. The same threats were made in open court, and the judge put Drake under the protection of a squad of special policemen.

Ryan's wife and two daughters testified that Drake had stood at the window, demanded Ryan's money and shot him. When defense attorney J. Hunt testified that Miss Ryan had told him the family did not know the attackers, spectators were so enraged that the judge placed Hunt under guard. After the jury first failed to agree, citizens declared that Drake and co-defendant Dan Cunningham would not leave the court house alive unless convicted, and opposing factions clashed and exchanged challenges. An Addison dispatch reported that many persons walked the streets of Spencer with shotguns and other weapons, threatening to kill Drake if he were acquitted.

The jury stayed out three days and failed to agree, eleven for conviction and one for acquittal according to the Spencer Bulletin. Defense lawyer S. C. Burdett said feeling against his client was very strong and expected the case to be moved to Kanawha County. In December Drake, under indictment by the Roane County grand jury, was brought before the court again, and his attorney won a postponement to the next term. No report of arrests among those who threatened him, or of a later verdict, was found.

Outside West Virginia the episode ran as sensational wire news: the New York Evening World headed its item "WANT TO LYNCH HIM IN COURT," and the Springfield Daily Republic ran "TO BE LYNCHED." Both called Drake an "alleged murderer" but repeated without comment the citizens' resolve to break up a "gang of thieves and toughs at any cost." The Evening World's headline also placed the trial at Parkersburg, the dateline, although its text put it at Spencer.

Within the state the Wheeling Intelligencer headed its dispatch "A Fine State of Affairs," and the Morgantown New Dominion reprinted it almost word for word in its state-news column. The local Spencer Bulletin, reprinted at Point Pleasant, reported only the jury split and said the trial had been watched by many thousand people. No report gave the race of Drake or of the crowd.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Perry Drake
bases: A mob tried to take Drake from officers and threatened to lynch him, and armed citizens threatened to kill him if acquitted, but no one was killed (A1, A2, A3).

A mob and armed citizens tried to seize and threatened to kill Drake, accused of the Ryan murder, outside any lawful process (A1, A2, A3), but no one was killed, so the episode is an attempted, not a completed, lynching.

Three separately datelined reports (Parkersburg A1, A2; Addison A3) agree that crowds threatened to kill Drake during his trial at Spencer; the attempted seizure on the way to court appears only in A1.

accounts.label: Parkersburg dispatch (Sept. 8)
accounts.gist: With the jury still out on Drake and Cunningham, citizens declared the two would not leave the court house alive unless convicted; factions clashed.

accounts.label: Addison dispatch / Spencer Bulletin
accounts.gist: The jury failed to agree, reportedly eleven to one for conviction, while armed men on the streets threatened to kill Drake if acquitted.

framing.detail: Out-of-state papers ran the Parkersburg dispatches under headlines such as 'WANT TO LYNCH HIM IN COURT' and 'TO BE LYNCHED', calling Drake an 'alleged murderer' and relaying the citizens' aim to break up a 'gang of thieves and toughs' without comment.
The Wheeling Intelligencer headed its item 'A Fine State of Affairs', an ironic note on the armed threats, while the Spencer Bulletin reported only the jury count.
